chapters.chapter_title: Unit 1: Learning Together (The Day the River Spoke & Try Again)

branches.theme: Prose Narrative: The Day the River Spoke

details: Lives in a coastal farming village in South India with her parents and three brothers.
Responsible for taking care of her baby brother Appu while parents work on the farm.
Calls her elder brother Gopi 'Ettan' (Malayalam for elder brother).
Longs to attend primary school like Gopi and her friend Meena, but feels paralyzed by fear of being 'too old' and chased away.
evidence_or_examples: Jahnavi weeping quietly at the riverbank while watching fishermen on catamarans.
Domestic responsibilities preventing her from enrolling at the standard starting age.

details: Harbors deep intellectual curiosity about biological and physical phenomena.
Questions why spiders turn yellow when sitting in yellow blossoms (camouflage).
Wonders why bamboo stalks rustle in the breeze and how tadpoles turn into frogs.
Ponders why the moon rises behind hills and where it disappears during the day.
evidence_or_examples: Observation of green lizards on rocks and kingfishers with blue arrow-like wings.
Nature serving as her primary observational learning environment.

details: The River speaks to Jahnavi before flowing to the sea, acting as a compassionate mentor.
Dismantles gender stereotypes by asserting that little girls swim as fast as little boys.
Encourages Jahnavi to take brave action rather than letting fear govern her choices.
Urges her to slip quietly into the schoolroom and sit down on the floor.
evidence_or_examples: The River saying: 'I've got to hurry to reach the sea, you know... tell me all about it.'
River's laughter at Jahnavi's groundless fears of teachers.

sub_branches.concept: Climax and Entry into Formal Schooling
details: Jahnavi overcomes her self-doubt, walks to the village school, and stands panting at the doorway.
Creeps quietly to the back row on the earthen floor with baby Appu sleeping on her shoulder.
Immerses herself in the teacher's lesson about Emperor Ashoka.
Marks her transition from passive exclusion to active participation in formal education.
evidence_or_examples: Carrying baby Appu into class, demonstrating that domestic duty and education can be harmonized.
Listening to the story of King Ashoka.

branches.theme: Narrative Poem: Try Again by Eliza Cook

details: King Bruce sits in a dark remote cave experiencing deep despair after six military defeats.
Contemplates abandoning his struggle to liberate Scotland from foreign rule.
Feels exhausted, hopeless, and ready to give up his royal purpose.
evidence_or_examples: King Bruce lying low on the cave floor contemplating defeat.

details: A spider drops down on a silken thread and attempts to climb back up to its web on the cave ceiling.
Falls nine consecutive times due to slippery conditions and gravity.
Persists without stopping or showing frustration.
Succeeds on its tenth attempt, successfully securing its thread to the web.
evidence_or_examples: The spider steadily mounting higher step by step after nine failed attempts.

details: The spider's struggle is used as an extended metaphor for human effort against difficult obstacles.
Employs alliteration in phrases like 'tried and tried' and 'season or snowy'.
King Bruce is inspired by the insect's success, rallies his army, and wins victory.
Delivers the universal moral imperative: 'If at first you don't succeed, try, try again.'
evidence_or_examples: King Bruce declaring that if an insect can strive nine times, a king cannot give up.

chapters.chapter_title: Unit 2: Wit and Humour (Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle & A Funny Man)

branches.theme: Prose Narrative: Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle (Hugh Lofting)

sub_branches.concept: Transition from Human Medicine to Veterinary Care
details: Dr. John Dolittle lives in Puddleby-on-the-Marsh and treats human patients who complain ungratefully.
The Cat's-food-Man suffers from a stomach-ache and suggests Dolittle become an animal doctor.
Argues that local veterinarians lack true understanding of animal ailments.
Dr. Dolittle loves animals and agrees that treating them would be far more fulfilling.
evidence_or_examples: The Cat's-food-Man pointing out that Dr. Dolittle knows more about animals than all local vets combined.

details: Polynesia the parrot reveals that animals possess complex languages comprising vocal phonetics and non-verbal signs.
Translates bird language: 'Ka-ka oi-ee, fee-fee' means 'Is the porridge hot yet?'.
Explains silent animal signetics: nose twitches, ear movements, tail wags, and eyelid flutters.
Dr. Dolittle gets his butcher's notebook and pen to systematically record animal vocabulary.
evidence_or_examples: Polynesia dusting cracker crumbs off her wing while teaching the doctor bird phonetics.
Dogs twitching their nostrils to ask questions without barking.

details: Dr. Dolittle opens a specialized clinic for domestic pets, working animals, and farm livestock.
Diagnoses pugs, poodles, cows, and plough horses by listening directly to their complaints in their own tongues.
Rejects generic veterinary remedies in favor of targeted, sympathetic treatments.
Gains widespread renown as a true animal scholar and master of inter-species communication.
evidence_or_examples: Old ladies bringing pugs sick from eating sweet cake; farmers bringing cows with eye troubles.

details: Classification of Compound Words into three distinct types:
1. Closed Compound Words: joined without spaces (windowsill, flowerpots, teatime).
2. Open Compound Words: written with spaces (bird language, plough horse, harvest mice).
3. Hyphenated Compound Words: joined by hyphens (Cat's-food-Man, check-in, well-bred).
Usage of present perfect tense for recent past actions with present relevance.
evidence_or_examples: Analyzing text examples across all three compound word categories.

branches.theme: Humorous Poem: A Funny Man by Natalie Joan

details: Describes an encounter with an extraordinarily eccentric figure.
The funny man wears two hats on his feet instead of shoes.
Walks and hops home balanced upside down on his head.
Eats a currant bun while staggering in an inverted posture.
evidence_or_examples: Visual contrast of shoes on head and hats covering feet.

details: Combines ridiculous physical appearance with formal, courtly speech.
Addresses the ordinary passerby speaker politely as 'Your Highness'.
Uses alliteration in phrases like 'funny sounding sight' and 'hopped home'.
Creates lighthearted wit through the juxtaposition of absurdity and formal manners.
evidence_or_examples: The funny man tipping his foot-hat while bowing and saying 'Good day, Your Highness'.

chapters.chapter_title: Unit 3: Dreams and Discoveries (My Brother's Great Invention & Paper Boats)

branches.theme: Prose Narrative: My Brother's Great Invention

details: Anand is a young aspiring inventor who constructs gadgets from scrap and household items.
Exhibits key traits of an inventor: curiosity, creativity, resourcefulness, determination, and resilience.
Constantly experiments despite family skepticism and initial mechanical failures.
evidence_or_examples: Gathering old pulleys, rubber water bags, copper wires, and strings to build devices.

sub_branches.concept: The Front-Door Burglar Alarm & Accidental Backfire
details: Anand designs a front-door alarm using a overhead pulley, string tripwire, and a heavy rubber water bag.
Intended to trigger a warning signal when the front door opens.
Mechanisms fails when Papa returns home exhausted after work and opens the entrance.
The tripwire releases the water bag directly overhead, soaking Papa completely and provoking family anger.
evidence_or_examples: Papa standing drenched on the doorstep while Ma scolds Anand for creating a wet mess.

details: Late at night, an actual burglar attempts to sneak into the house through the front entrance.
The burglar trips Anand's door mechanism, dropping heavy objects and raising a loud alarm.
The unexpected noise frightens the intruder away and wakes up the household.
Validates Anand's inventive concept, proving that trial-and-error leads to effective real-world solutions.
evidence_or_examples: The thief fleeing into the night after triggering Anand's contraptions.

branches.theme: Poem: Paper Boats by Rabindranath Tagore

sub_branches.concept: Childhood Play & Message Sending across Distance
details: A young child floats paper boats down a running stream day after day.
Writes his name and the name of his village on each boat in big black letters.
Hopes that people living in distant, unknown lands will find his boats and learn who he is.
Reflects the universal childhood longing for identity, connection, and friendship beyond immediate borders.
evidence_or_examples: Writing 'big black letters' on paper boat hulls before launching them downstream.

details: Loads his paper boats with fresh white shiuli (parijat) blossoms gathered from his garden at dawn.
Wishes that these delicate morning flowers will be carried safely to land in the night.
Looks up at the sky and compares floating white clouds to the bulging sails of his paper boats.
Uses visual, tactile, and olfactory sensory imagery to enhance the poetic atmosphere.
evidence_or_examples: Shiuli blossoms blooming at dawn placed inside folded paper hulls.
White clouds sailing in the sky like bulging paper sails.

details: At night, the child buries his face in his arms and dreams of his paper boats under midnight stars.
Imagines that 'fairies of sleep' are sailing in his boats across celestial waters.
Envisions the boats loaded with cargo consisting of 'baskets full of dreams'.
Transforms simple physical play into an uplifting spiritual and imaginative fantasy.
evidence_or_examples: Burying his face in his arms at bedtime to dream of night fairies guiding his boats.

chapters.chapter_title: Unit 4: Travel and Adventure (The Tunnel by Ruskin Bond & Travel)

sub_branches.concept: Suraj's Exploration & The Steam Engine Metaphor
details: Young Suraj cycles out of town, leaves his bicycle at a scrub village, and walks to a deep forest railway cutting.
Waits at the horseshoe masonry arch not to ride the train, but to experience its sensory arrival.
Views the steam locomotive as a magnificent 'green, black, and gold dragon, snorting and puffing, showering sparks'.
Demonstrates pure childhood adventure, wonder, and fascination with heavy machinery.
evidence_or_examples: Suraj standing on the high embankment watching steam plumes burst from the tunnel.

details: Sunder Singh is the solitary railway watchman living in a small hut near the cutting.
Walks the entire length of the dark tunnel before every train to inspect tracks for rockfalls or animals.
Maintains strict safety protocols: green flag/lamp for clear tracks, red flag/lamp for danger.
Views his job as a solemn responsibility to protect human lives and forest wildlife.
evidence_or_examples: Sunder Singh carrying his oil lamp, red flag, and axe into the dark tunnel.

details: A wild leopard uses the dark tunnel as its shelter during hot days.
Sunder Singh explains that the leopard knows him well and preys on stray goats rather than humans.
When the night mail train approaches at 9 p.m., Sunder Singh enters the tunnel with his axe and lamp.
Shouts and makes noise to drive the leopard safely into the surrounding brush before the train roars through.
evidence_or_examples: Driving the leopard off the tracks so it will not be struck and killed by the night mail.

details: Suraj later boards the night train with his family and looks back into the dark cutting.
Sees Sunder Singh holding his glowing oil lamp—a solitary 'firefly' lighting up the forest night.
Symbolizes how small, humble human acts of duty illuminate vast darkness.
Grammar Focus: Use of 'would' + base verb to express habitual past actions (e.g., 'Sunder Singh would walk the tunnel').
evidence_or_examples: Suraj seeing the small yellow light of Sunder Singh's lamp receding in the dark jungle.

branches.theme: Reflective Poem: Travel by Edna St. Vincent Millay

sub_branches.concept: Wanderlust & The Universal Call of Exploration
details: Expresses an inescapable, deep-seated longing to travel and see distant places.
Regardless of daily human warmth, quiet conversations, or comfortable surroundings, the speaker's mind drifts.
Hearing a distant train whistle at night immediately triggers intense wanderlust.
Uses auditory imagery ('whistle shrieking') and visual imagery ('cinders red on the sky') to capture the romance of railways.
evidence_or_examples: The speaker stating that no matter what friends are speaking during the day, night train whistles compel her thoughts.

chapters.chapter_title: Unit 5: Bravehearts (A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers & My Dear Soldiers)

branches.theme: Prose Narrative: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers

details: Soumya writes a letter to her friend Ananda describing her school tour to the National War Memorial in New Delhi.
Features a central 15-meter tall Obelisk and the eternal flame (Amar Jawan Jyoti).
Built with four concentric circular rings:
1. Amar Chakra (Circle of Immortality): Central obelisk and eternal flame.
2. Veerta Chakra (Circle of Bravery): Depicts crucial battle murals.
3. Tyag Chakra (Circle of Sacrifice): Granite walls with golden lettering bearing names of fallen soldiers.
4. Rakshak Chakra (Circle of Protection): Dense ring of trees representing guarding soldiers.
evidence_or_examples: Granite tablets lined with thousands of names of fallen heroes since 1947.

details: Chronicles specific bravehearts who made the supreme sacrifice:
Major Somnath Sharma: First recipient of the Param Vir Chakra (PVC); defended Badgam airbase in 1947 with a plastered arm.
Captain Mahendra Nath Mulla: Maha Vir Chakra (MVC); gave his lifejacket to a young sailor and went down with INS Khukri in 1971.
Lance Naik Albert Ekka: PVC; silenced enemy machine-gun bunkers in 1971 despite mortal wounds.
Major Padmapani Acharya: MVC; led his platoon up steep cliffs under heavy fire to capture Tololing Knoll during the 1999 Kargil War.
evidence_or_examples: Captain Mulla surrendering his lifejacket to save a junior crew member.

details: Ananda's reply translates feelings of national pride into concrete action.
Pledges to download the National War Memorial mobile app to research local heroes.
Plans to construct school wall collages, write gratitude notes, and present stories in class.
Demonstrates how commemorating fallen heroes inspires young citizens to embrace duty and patriotism.
evidence_or_examples: Ananda creating a school exhibition board on gallantry award winners.

branches.theme: Patriotic Poem: My Dear Soldiers by Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam

details: Salutes servicemen and servicewomen guarding national sovereignty across brutal terrains.
Defending snowy mountain glaciers, sweltering desert sands, coastal marshes, deep seas, and high skies.
Maintains continuous alertness while citizens sleep peacefully in their homes.
Refers to soldiers as 'great sons of my land' who dedicate the prime of their youth to the nation.
evidence_or_examples: Soldiers guarding Siachen glaciers in freezing temperatures and Rajasthan deserts in scorching heat.

details: Employs the simile 'treading the lonely expanses as yogis' to capture soldiers' ascetic self-discipline.
Highlights their detachment from personal comforts and solitary focus on duty.
Concludes with a national prayer asking for divine protection, health, and blessings for armed forces personnel.
evidence_or_examples: Comparing border patrol isolation to the quiet, disciplined life of a yogi.
